name: Elena Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a small diesel van I bought cheap at auction, and I run two apps across the valley: parcels in the day, takeaway at night. The villages are spread out, so it's a lot of miles for not much. I'm still getting the hang of it; I took a wrong turn up the quarry road last week and lost forty minutes. I start at nine and finish when the curry house on the square closes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's mine, nobody watching me. I use AI apps every day, to plan which villages to stack, to keep my books, even to draft a little flyer. The hard bit is the money, diesel eats half of what I make. I live with my partner Arjun, who works in his family's corner shop, and we've got about two weeks of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the tools are still handy, I'll keep using them. People who panicked can relax. The work's still there for anyone willing to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means nothing changes, and nothing changing isn't great either. I'm paying for diesel and the van's MOT, the yearly safety test, out of very thin pay. I want something more than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running both apps and use AI to cut wasted miles. I'd try to start a small delivery service of my own, for the village shops that the big apps don't bother with. I'd save every bit I can for a second-hand electric van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless and a bit worried. Mostly restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two weeks of money is tight. What keeps you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van. If the gearbox goes, I'm off the road and we're both living on Arjun's shop wages. In a valley with no other delivery work, losing the van means losing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a flyer. What was that for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A local delivery round for the village shops: the butcher, the bakery, Arjun's family's shop. Old folk up the valley can't get to town. If I could get six shops paying a weekly fee, I'd be my own boss.

say: The **tools are handy**, and I'll keep using them.
The work's still there for **anyone willing** to do it.
think: Nothing changing **isn't great** either, on my thin pay.
**Diesel and the MOT** eat my earnings; I want more than this.
do: Use **AI planning** to cut wasted valley miles.
Start a **village shop delivery** service for a weekly fee.
S0.quote: In a valley with no other delivery work, losing the van means losing the job.
fieldNote: Her **entrepreneurial streak** is strong: she wants her own village round.
Uses **AI daily** for routes, books and flyers.
Thin savings make a **van breakdown** her main fear.

steps.text: Use AI route planning to cut wasted valley miles
Sign up six village shops for a weekly delivery round
Save towards a second-hand electric van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the tools, they're on our side if you use them. Small businesses can do more with less now. I'd post about my village round to show what one person can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this suits me. The planning and books get done for me, so I can spend my time on the driving and customers. The big apps would squeeze the drivers harder, but I'd be building my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the village round properly, with AI handling the bookings and the reminders. I'd keep one app going for steady money. I'd ask the bank about a small loan for the electric van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Most of your job is driving, but you also plan routes and do your books. What does AI take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking bits: the planning, the booking, the invoices. That's the boring bit for me. What's left is the van and the doorstep, and I'm getting better at both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Arjun's family make of your idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's dad thinks I'm mad, but the corner shop needs deliveries to survive. If my round works, the shop gets a delivery service without paying a big app's fees.

**Small businesses** can do more with less now, and I'd post my round.
think: This **suits me**, since AI takes my planning and books.
Big apps would squeeze drivers, but I'd be **building my own** thing.
do: Launch the **village round** with AI bookings and reminders.
Ask the bank about a **small loan** for an electric van.
feel: **Excited**, a little nervous about the loan.
S1.quote: My partner's dad thinks I'm mad, but the corner shop needs deliveries to survive.
fieldNote: She sees thinking AI as **taking the boring parts**, freeing her for driving and customers.
Debt for a van is a **real risk** on two weeks of savings.
Her plan helps **Arjun's family's shop**, tying business to family.

steps.text: Run village round bookings and reminders through an AI app
Keep the parcel app for steady income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will have to roll up their sleeves, because nobody's coming to save us. Families and towns will have to pull together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI side makes my small business easier at first. Then around 2031 the robots come for the driving, and the big firms will have robot vans in the valley before I do. My round could be beaten by a robot that doesn't need a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the village round fast in the three years, so the shops are mine before the robot vans arrive. I'd save to buy a delivery robot or drone myself, instead of being replaced by one. I'd keep the debt small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The window is small and I've got no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028, then robots around 2031. What do those three years mean for your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years. I'd rather become the business that owns the delivery robot than the driver it replaces. I'd need the customers to trust me more than they'd trust a big firm, and that's my only edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Arjun?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Arjun we need to put every spare pound into the business and hold off on the wedding. His mum won't like that.

say: People must **roll up their sleeves**; nobody's coming to save us.
**Families and towns** will have to pull together.
think: AI first makes my **small business easier**.
Robot vans from **big firms** could reach the valley before me around 2031.
do: Grow the **village round** fast within three years.
Save to buy my own **delivery robot or drone**.
Hold off the **wedding** to fund the business.
feel: **Alarmed**: the window is small and I have no cushion.
S2.quote: I'd rather become the business that owns the delivery robot than the driver it replaces.
fieldNote: She uses the **three-year gap** to build a customer base before robots arrive.
Wants to **own automation**, not be replaced by it.
Her **thin savings** make the plan risky and keep her alarmed.

steps.text: Sign up every village shop in the valley within three years
Buy a delivery drone or robot for the round
Put every spare pound into the business fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair chance for anyone with some get-up-and-go. Use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I can build the round slowly, AGI in 2031 and robots around 2034. I'd still be small, but I'd have regulars. The risk is getting the timing of buying robots wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run the village round alongside one app for two years. Then buy an electric van and drop the apps. I'd learn how the delivery drones work, maybe get a drone licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I like a challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years make the plan safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, yes. Buying a delivery robot too early means debt on a machine that's out of date, and buying too late means the big firms beat me. Five years gives me room to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robot vans from the big firms are cheaper than anything I can afford. If they undercut me, my regulars might stay loyal for a bit, but not forever.

say: **Five years** is a fair chance for anyone with some get-up-and-go.
People should **use the time** rather than sit and wait.
think: I can build the round **slowly** with five years.
The risk is getting the **timing** of buying robots wrong.
do: Run the **village round** alongside one app for two years.
Buy an **electric van** and drop the apps.
Get a **drone licence** and learn how delivery drones work.
S3.quote: Buying a delivery robot too early means debt on a machine that's out of date, and buying too late means the big firms beat me.
fieldNote: Five years shifts her from rush to **careful timing**.
She's thinking like a **small business owner** about capital risk.
Still anxious because **big firms** can undercut her.

steps.text: Run the village round alongside one delivery app
Buy an electric van and drop the apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time for a business to get ready. Anyone who complains with ten years' warning wasn't going to change anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when the robots come in 2039. That's time to build the round, get married, maybe start a family. It's the best version for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build the village round over three years, buy the electric van, then add a drone or robot when they're proven. Marry Arjun in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit uneasy about the money right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Where would you want to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a small delivery business in the valley, with a couple of robots and one or two people. Married, with the shop still open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year's diesel and the van's gearbox. Ten years is a lovely idea, but a broken gearbox would sink me next month.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time** for a business to get ready.
Anyone complaining with that warning **wasn't going** to change anyway.
think: I'd be **37** when the robots arrive in 2039.
This is the **best version** for me: business, marriage, family.
do: Build the **village round** over three years.
Buy an **electric van**, then add a proven robot or drone.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, uneasy about money right now.
S4.quote: Ten years is a lovely idea, but a broken gearbox would sink me next month.
fieldNote: Ten years is her **ideal timeline**, aligning business and family plans.
Present-day **van costs** keep her from feeling calm.
Shows a **traditional** mix of enterprise and marriage.

steps.text: Build the valley village round over three years
Buy an electric van for the round
Add a proven delivery robot or drone later
Marry Arjun while the business grows

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to build my own thing before the big firms' robots arrive. What would help is cheap small-business loans and a rule that local firms can use the same robots at a fair price.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether small people get a fair go at the robots. Everyone assumes robots belong to the big companies, but I'd like a valley girl with a van to own one too.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes robots belong to the big companies, but I'd like a valley girl with a van to own one too.
portrait: Elena is **27**, drives a cheap auction van for two apps across a spread-out valley.
She uses **AI daily** for routes, books and flyers, and is restless for more.
She plans a **village delivery round** for local shops, including her partner's family shop.
Her aim is to **own the robots**, not be replaced by them, though thin savings make it risky.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to build her business before big firms' robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **small-business loans** and fair access to **robots** for local firms.
